[{:db/id 17592186198369 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b5a18f4e-2d75-5904-b5e5-ab7ba2838493"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198384 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3e5df847-265a-5b9c-9720-3136b8ccb366" "question-fa0b27c3-d4dd-5c0c-8989-66af8729df06"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198377 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ff752515-0aa8-5668-9f6f-2eed5f67dc87" "question-22e295c4-59c2-57da-8c38-5051b16dc6ee"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198375 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b54a0f96-7cef-5900-9667-b793d1ee0611" "question-9b6d5f3b-6c7c-587f-b086-0bc40be20551"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198017 :question/worked-solution "For our transformation $\mathbf{T},$ we have

$$
x = u \cos v, \qquad y = u \sin v.
$$

Notice that if we change $u$ to $r$ and $v$ to $\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

which represents the usual formulas for changing from polar to Cartesian coordinates. 

Therefore, the pre-image $\Delta$ of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that can be written as 

$$
\Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  \sqrt 2 \le u \le 3, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{12}  \leq v \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6} \bigg\}.
$$

This is the rectangular region enclosed between

- two vertical lines with Cartesian equations $u=\sqrt 2$ and $u=3,$ and

- two horizontal lines with Cartesian equations $v=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ and $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/c8/c83bd9d913d4959ad275ab4420b647cd030fff45438f59d026e3658bd146a1ee.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278346 :question/problem "![](images/04/0412da40e0e04e8da5ec92db1ad665251209a718333ec008ceeebbe308c71855.png)

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{4}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the left side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186389098 :question/problem "![](images/6e/6e0e9b7d2cbff011a5ff209f335fb3d5e86af02a58c4ea5c8a8d46bd384e6a0c.png)

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le \sqrt{3},\,\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the right side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b5a18f4e-2d75-5904-b5e5-ab7ba2838493" :question/id #uuid "b5a18f4e-2d75-5904-b5e5-ab7ba2838493" :question/math-academy-id "q-160968" :question/problem "![](images/93/93132c9352ed5068001c824741a1c0a7cb8dca82564ad91db706bc1ecfcedbcc.png)

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 6,\,\,\frac{14\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{11\pi }{6}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the right side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the right side.

For the right side, we have $u=6$ and $\frac{14\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{11\pi }{6}.$ 

Substituting $u=6$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(6\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{14\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{11\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an equation of a circular arc of radius $6$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. 
The arc lies in the fourth quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{14\pi }{9}$ and $\theta =\frac{11\pi }{6},$ as shown below.

![](images/b6/b6052c625de5a1d392975afae8c1053b2b430859ba6fbc3bc8c2c3de01d40318.png)" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields "![](images/29/2932639855f3031da6adcca7eaee38b992a145809f119902e93958fee47ff2a6.png)

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the left side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278350 :question/problem "![](images/21/21952fe273fd1a1ecb03727f4aa254d4e0ecdab2feaeb1d8c652bc9923404846.png)

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 4,\,\,\frac{13\pi }{12}\le v\le \frac{13\pi }{9}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the left side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-3e5df847-265a-5b9c-9720-3136b8ccb366" :question/id #uuid "3e5df847-265a-5b9c-9720-3136b8ccb366" :question/math-academy-id "q-161024" :question/problem "![](images/a4/a44852c606e67842a58ad1a696253e6e211816f8243beec8b3eea97ef42055a2.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{4\pi }{9}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v=\frac{4\pi }{9}$ and $\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{4\pi }{9}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{9}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{9})),\,\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment that makes an angle of $\frac{4\pi }{9}$ with the positive $x$-axis and whose endpoints lie on circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $3$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

"![](images/aa/aa62dda1abb7bc6bca1b2e6cdf356b52946820912ec6318e5901273a546ee96a.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,\,\frac{3\pi }{4}\le v\le \frac{7\pi }{6}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the bottom side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fa0b27c3-d4dd-5c0c-8989-66af8729df06" :question/id #uuid "fa0b27c3-d4dd-5c0c-8989-66af8729df06" :question/math-academy-id "q-161029" :question/problem "![](images/12/1252844f7a9e2fb2ca0ff1d2e2e1546a460e7d0846b4ae2996b6ce984ee305a1.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1,\,\,0\le v\le \frac{5\pi }{12}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

I. The image makes the angle of $0$ with the positive $x$-axis.

II. The image makes the angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

III. The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1$ centered at $O.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ and $\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/49/49aa7d6ccd4b14b48ede7486f41ab11ac22b593c06d75795fe7819889b2b2f23.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement III is true.

- When $u=\frac{1}{4},$ we obtain the point 
$(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $\frac{1}{4}.$

- When $u=1,$ we obtain the point 
$(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $1.$

So, the endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f7528fa6-219c-52b3-82fe-4826326f572d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f7528fa6-219c-52b3-82fe-4826326f572d" :answer-field/id #uuid "f7528fa6-219c-52b3-82fe-4826326f572d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-45672c57-a19d-5a8b-ac6b-6ea21293b5d7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d1969766-6b47-59dc-a429-472653bbb6d3" "answer-c03a15a1-3e13-53ce-9c92-762f8bc2417d" "answer-45672c57-a19d-5a8b-ac6b-6ea21293b5d7" "answer-cc45f2dd-0a53-53f5-b140-3b2a83fa50cc" "answer-97210339-8c0b-5905-a2df-f3b57f435e8f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d1969766-6b47-59dc-a429-472653bbb6d3" :answer/id #uuid "d1969766-6b47-59dc-a429-472653bbb6d3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c03a15a1-3e13-53ce-9c92-762f8bc2417d" :answer/id #uuid "c03a15a1-3e13-53ce-9c92-762f8bc2417d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-45672c57-a19d-5a8b-ac6b-6ea21293b5d7" :answer/id #uuid "45672c57-a19d-5a8b-ac6b-6ea21293b5d7" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cc45f2dd-0a53-53f5-b140-3b2a83fa50cc" :answer/id #uuid "cc45f2dd-0a53-53f5-b140-3b2a83fa50cc" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-97210339-8c0b-5905-a2df-f3b57f435e8f" :answer/id #uuid "97210339-8c0b-5905-a2df-f3b57f435e8f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198580 :question/problem "![](images/b8/b8874b14fa80881e69cb1daee180d2e342a27c5902e66fc75d43622278176b09.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the bottom side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

I. The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

II. The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

III. The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278355 :question/problem "![](images/16/16d74107dbbf12749766cd9cea7e38d16e28a59efb997bd224aed73c7830324e.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 4,\,\,\frac{10\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{4\pi }{3}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

I. The image makes the angle of $\frac{10\pi }{9}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

II. The image makes the angle of $\frac{4\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

III. The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $2$ centered at $O.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186389077 :question/problem "![](images/95/951c3d3bca4116deebccbbabb5d7405bb07669cacb83c1e450204bb40c247d5c.png)

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\sqrt{2}\le u\le 2,\,\,\frac{\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{2\pi }{5}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Find the image of $Δ$ under the action of $T.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ff752515-0aa8-5668-9f6f-2eed5f67dc87" :question/id #uuid "ff752515-0aa8-5668-9f6f-2eed5f67dc87" :question/math-academy-id "q-160924" :question/problem "![](images/19/19f21fa7abb989e8c2bf35552675f498969e30e1f42012fd615c00686d20cb01.png)

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,\,\frac{3\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{6\pi }{7}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Find the image of $Δ$ under the action of $T.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $Δ$ separately:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\frac{3\pi }{5}$ and $1\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{3\pi }{5}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{5}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{5})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{3\pi }{5}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\frac{6\pi }{7}$ and $1\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{6\pi }{7}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{7}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{7})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{6\pi }{7}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\frac{3\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{6\pi }{7}.$ 

Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{5\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\frac{7\pi }{4}$ and $\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{7\pi }{4}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{7\pi }{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=\sqrt{2}$ and $\frac{5\pi }{3}\le v\le \frac{7\pi }{4}.$ 

Substituting $u=\sqrt{2}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{3}$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}.$

- Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=3$ and $\frac{5\pi }{3}\le v\le \frac{7\pi }{4}.$ 

Substituting $u=3$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(3\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

- two circles with polar equations $r=\sqrt{2}$ and $r=3,$ and

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$

$$

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\sqrt{2}\le u\le 4,\,\,\frac{7\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{9\pi }{5}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Find the image of $Δ$ under the action of $T.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b54a0f96-7cef-5900-9667-b793d1ee0611" :question/id #uuid "b54a0f96-7cef-5900-9667-b793d1ee0611" :question/math-academy-id "q-160947" :question/problem "![](images/16/1686ee5f02ab2215b700216f8dd0844d4763d0f3bde9837cb7913d2790a9c310.png)

Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, shown above. The transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),\,y(u,v)),
$$

where

$$
x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,
$$

maps the region $Δ$ from the $uv$-plane to $D.$ Which of the following could be the region $Δ?$" :question/worked-solution "For our transformation $T,$ we have

$$
x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v.
$$

Notice that if we change $u$ to $r$ and $v$ to $\theta ,$ we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

which represents the usual formulas for changing from polar to Cartesian coordinates. 

Therefore, the pre-image $Δ$ of $D$ under the action of $T$ is the region that can be written as 

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \frac{3}{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

This is the rectangular region enclosed between

- two vertical lines with Cartesian equations $u=1$ and $u=\frac{3}{2},$ and

- two horizontal lines with Cartesian equations $v=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{2},$

as shown in the diagram below.

{:db/id 17592186199463 :tutorial/content "Consider the rectangular region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
\Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  1 \le u \le 2, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5} \bigg\}
$$

and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

A sketch of $\Delta$ is shown below.

![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

     

To find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ onto the $xy$-plane, we need to transform each side (bottom, top, left, and right) of $\Delta$ separately: 

![](images/06/062a3d1f13e8566770118650c92231ebe17f5eba2b4ae8d8b41722e33a72baff.png)

It can be shown that $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$ So, let's proceed to find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ by mapping these four sides." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199475 :tutorial/content "![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

  

Our goal is to find the image of the region $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Let's first find the images of the horizontal sides:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$ Substituting $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})).\end{aligned}
$$

This represents a line segment that lies on a line passing through the origin. The slope of this line must be

$$
k = \dfrac{\sin \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)}{\cos \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)} = \tan\bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg),
$$

meaning that the line makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. 
The endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/ca/ca644fa90870697e9cea1740c6432d43f682c650521217f19ea6f87c09cba0fd.png)

- Similarly, we can find the image of the top side, where $v=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$

![](images/11/118c9d18e4d8158014643771c9fa018b1b15da38184f693b89d07f9fadd3c748.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199476 :tutorial/content "![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

  

Our transformation $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Let's now find the images of the vertical lines:

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5}.$ Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{5},$ as shown below.

![](images/2e/2e0e5a723b7a9fdc860bcf3f619b6db4bdbec24c06bc22f3121a620080969b6c.png)

- Similarly, we can find the image of the right side, where we have $u=2$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5}.$

![](images/c1/c1b9f163724e97d662192d5d274768b3e501843a2a2267adc5a3e1f5c6c9d230.png)

Therefore, the image $D$ of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=2,$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{5},$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/04/048606038e26fe79430899c284beff24921397879bb0ce5d46ab1f3653cab47e.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198481 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
x = u \cos v, \qquad y = u \sin v.
$$

Notice that if we change $u$ to $r$ and $v$ to $\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

which represents the usual formulas for changing from polar to Cartesian coordinates. 

Therefore, the pre-image $\Delta$ of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that can be written as 

$$
\Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  \sqrt 2 \le u \le 3, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{12}  \leq v \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6} \bigg\}.
$$

This is the rectangular region enclosed between

- two vertical lines with Cartesian equations $u=\sqrt 2$ and $u=3,$ and

- two horizontal lines with Cartesian equations $v=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ and $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$

as shown in the diagram below.

Which of the following could be the image of the right side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the right side.

For the right side, we have $u=6$ and $\frac{14\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{11\pi }{6}.$ 

Substituting $u=6$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(6\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{14\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{11\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an equation of a circular arc of radius $6$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. 
The arc lies in the fourth quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{14\pi }{9}$ and $\theta =\frac{11\pi }{6},$ as shown below.

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{4\pi }{9}\},
$$

$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment that makes an angle of $\frac{4\pi }{9}$ with the positive $x$-axis and whose endpoints lie on circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $3$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

"![](images/aa/aa62dda1abb7bc6bca1b2e6cdf356b52946820912ec6318e5901273a546ee96a.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,\,\frac{3\pi }{4}\le v\le \frac{7\pi }{6}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the bottom side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fa0b27c3-d4dd-5c0c-8989-66af8729df06" :question/id #uuid "fa0b27c3-d4dd-5c0c-8989-66af8729df06" :question/math-academy-id "q-161029" :question/problem "![](images/12/1252844f7a9e2fb2ca0ff1d2e2e1546a460e7d0846b4ae2996b6ce984ee305a1.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1,\,\,0\le v\le \frac{5\pi }{12}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

I. The image makes the angle of $0$ with the positive $x$-axis.

II. The image makes the angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

III. The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1$ centered at $O.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ and $\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/49/49aa7d6ccd4b14b48ede7486f41ab11ac22b593c06d75795fe7819889b2b2f23.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement III is true.

- When $u=\frac{1}{4},$ we obtain the point 
$(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $\frac{1}{4}.$

- When $u=1,$ we obtain the point 
$(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $1.$

So, the endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1.$

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the bottom side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

I. The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

II. The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

III. The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186278355 :question/problem "![](images/16/16d74107dbbf12749766cd9cea7e38d16e28a59efb997bd224aed73c7830324e.png)

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 4,\,\,\frac{10\pi }{9}\le v\le \frac{4\pi }{3}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

I. The image makes the angle of $\frac{10\pi }{9}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

II. The image makes the angle of $\frac{4\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

III. The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $2$ centered at $O.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186389077 :question/problem "![](images/95/951c3d3bca4116deebccbbabb5d7405bb07669cacb83c1e450204bb40c247d5c.png)

and the transformation $T,$ given by

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,\,\frac{3\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{6\pi }{7}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Find the image of $Δ$ under the action of $T.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $Δ$ separately:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\frac{3\pi }{5}$ and $1\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{3\pi }{5}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{5}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{5})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{3\pi }{5}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\frac{6\pi }{7}$ and $1\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{6\pi }{7}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{7}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{7})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{6\pi }{7}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\frac{3\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{6\pi }{7}.$ 

Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{6\pi }{7}.$

- Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=3$ and $\frac{3\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{6\pi }{7}.$ 

Substituting $u=3$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(3\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{6\pi }{7}.$

Therefore, the image $D$ of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=3,$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{6\pi }{7},$

as shown in the diagram below.

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\sqrt{2}\le u\le 4,\,\,\frac{7\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{9\pi }{5}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, shown above. The transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),\,y(u,v)),
$$

where

$$
x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,
$$

maps the region $Δ$ from the $uv$-plane to $D.$ Which of the following could be the region $Δ?$" :question/worked-solution "For our transformation $T,$ we have

$$
x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v.
$$

Notice that if we change $u$ to $r$ and $v$ to $\theta ,$ we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

which represents the usual formulas for changing from polar to Cartesian coordinates. 

Therefore, the pre-image $Δ$ of $D$ under the action of $T$ is the region that can be written as 

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \frac{3}{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

This is the rectangular region enclosed between

- two vertical lines with Cartesian equations $u=1$ and $u=\frac{3}{2},$ and

- two horizontal lines with Cartesian equations $v=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{2},$

as shown in the diagram below.

{:db/id 17592186199463 :tutorial/content "Consider the rectangular region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
\Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  1 \le u \le 2, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5} \bigg\}
$$

and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

A sketch of $\Delta$ is shown below.

![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

     

To find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ onto the $xy$-plane, we need to transform each side (bottom, top, left, and right) of $\Delta$ separately: 

![](images/06/062a3d1f13e8566770118650c92231ebe17f5eba2b4ae8d8b41722e33a72baff.png)

It can be shown that $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$ So, let's proceed to find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ by mapping these four sides." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199475 :tutorial/content "![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

  

Our goal is to find the image of the region $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Let's first find the images of the horizontal sides:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$ Substituting $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})).\end{aligned}
$$

This represents a line segment that lies on a line passing through the origin. The slope of this line must be

$$
k = \dfrac{\sin \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)}{\cos \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)} = \tan\bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg),
$$

meaning that the line makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. 
The endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/ca/ca644fa90870697e9cea1740c6432d43f682c650521217f19ea6f87c09cba0fd.png)

- Similarly, we can find the image of the top side, where $v=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$

![](images/11/118c9d18e4d8158014643771c9fa018b1b15da38184f693b89d07f9fadd3c748.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199476 :tutorial/content "![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

  

Our transformation $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Let's now find the images of the vertical lines:

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5}.$ Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{5},$ as shown below.

![](images/2e/2e0e5a723b7a9fdc860bcf3f619b6db4bdbec24c06bc22f3121a620080969b6c.png)

- Similarly, we can find the image of the right side, where we have $u=2$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5}.$

![](images/c1/c1b9f163724e97d662192d5d274768b3e501843a2a2267adc5a3e1f5c6c9d230.png)

Therefore, the image $D$ of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=2,$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{5},$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/04/048606038e26fe79430899c284beff24921397879bb0ce5d46ab1f3653cab47e.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198481 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186198017 :question/worked-solution "For our transformation $\mathbf{T},$ we have

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1,\,\,0\le v\le \frac{5\pi }{12}\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the top side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

I. The image makes the angle of $0$ with the positive $x$-axis.

II. The image makes the angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ with the positive $x$-axis.

III. The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1$ centered at $O.$"] ["question-fa0b27c3-d4dd-5c0c-8989-66af8729df06" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ and $\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{5\pi }{12}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/49/49aa7d6ccd4b14b48ede7486f41ab11ac22b593c06d75795fe7819889b2b2f23.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{5\pi }{12}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement III is true.

- When $u=\frac{1}{4},$ we obtain the point 
$(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $\frac{1}{4}.$

- When $u=1,$ we obtain the point 
$(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{12})),$
whose distance to the origin is $1.$

So, the endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $\frac{1}{4}$ and $1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-fa0b27c3-d4dd-5c0c-8989-66af8729df06" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] - Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\frac{6\pi }{7}$ and $1\le u\le 3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}

Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3,\,\,\frac{5\pi }{3}\le v\le \frac{7\pi }{4}\},
$$

$$

$$

Find the image of $Δ$ under the action of $T.$"] ["question-22e295c4-59c2-57da-8c38-5051b16dc6ee" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $Δ$ separately:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\frac{5\pi }{3}$ and $\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{5\pi }{3}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{5\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\frac{7\pi }{4}$ and $\sqrt{2}\le u\le 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{7\pi }{4}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{4})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{7\pi }{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $\sqrt{2}$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=\sqrt{2}$ and $\frac{5\pi }{3}\le v\le \frac{7\pi }{4}.$ 

Substituting $u=\sqrt{2}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{3}$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}.$

- Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=3$ and $\frac{5\pi }{3}\le v\le \frac{7\pi }{4}.$ 

Substituting $u=3$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(3\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{3}$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4}.$

Therefore, the image $D$ of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=\sqrt{2}$ and $r=3,$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{3}$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{4},$

as shown in the diagram below.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}

$$

This is the rectangular region enclosed between

- two vertical lines with Cartesian equations $u=1$ and $u=\frac{3}{2},$ and

\Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  1 \le u \le 2, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5} \bigg\}
$$

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

A sketch of $\Delta$ is shown below.

![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

     

To find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ onto the $xy$-plane, we need to transform each side (bottom, top, left, and right) of $\Delta$ separately: 

![](images/06/062a3d1f13e8566770118650c92231ebe17f5eba2b4ae8d8b41722e33a72baff.png)

Our goal is to find the image of the region $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Let's first find the images of the horizontal sides:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$ Substituting $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})).\end{aligned}
$$

This represents a line segment that lies on a line passing through the origin. The slope of this line must be

$$
k = \dfrac{\sin \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)}{\cos \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)} = \tan\bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg),
$$

meaning that the line makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. 
The endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/ca/ca644fa90870697e9cea1740c6432d43f682c650521217f19ea6f87c09cba0fd.png)

- Similarly, we can find the image of the top side, where $v=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$

![](images/11/118c9d18e4d8158014643771c9fa018b1b15da38184f693b89d07f9fadd3c748.png)"] [17592186199476 :tutorial/content "![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

  

Our transformation $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Let's now find the images of the vertical lines:

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5}.$ Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{5},$ as shown below.

![](images/2e/2e0e5a723b7a9fdc860bcf3f619b6db4bdbec24c06bc22f3121a620080969b6c.png)

- Similarly, we can find the image of the right side, where we have $u=2$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5}.$

![](images/c1/c1b9f163724e97d662192d5d274768b3e501843a2a2267adc5a3e1f5c6c9d230.png)

Therefore, the image $D$ of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=2,$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{5},$

as shown in the diagram below.

Consider the rectangular region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  1 \le u \le 2, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \right\},
$$

and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Determine the image of the right side of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $\Delta$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the right side.

For the right side, we have $u = 2$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$ 

Substituting $u = 2$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le v\le \frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an equation of a circular arc of radius $2$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. 
The arc lies in the first and second quadrants between the polar rays $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ as shown below.

Consider the rectangular region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le \sqrt{3},\,\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Which of the following could be the image of the right side of $Δ$ under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the right side.

For the right side, we have $u=\sqrt{3}$ and $0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Substituting $u=\sqrt{3}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an equation of a circular arc of radius $\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. 
The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown below.

Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, shown above. The transformation $\mathbf{T},$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (x(u,v) , \, y(u,v)),
$$

where

$$
x = u \cos v, \qquad y= u \sin v,
$$

maps the region $\Delta$ from the $uv$-plane to $D.$ Sketch the region $\Delta.$" :question/worked-solution "For our transformation $\mathbf{T},$ we have

$$
x = u \cos v, \qquad y = u \sin v.
$$

Notice that if we change $u$ to $r$ and $v$ to $\theta,$ we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

which represents the usual formulas for changing from polar to Cartesian coordinates. 

Therefore, the pre-image $\Delta$ of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that can be written as 

$$
\Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  \sqrt 2 \le u \le 3, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{12}  \leq v \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6} \bigg\}.
$$

This is the rectangular region enclosed between

- two vertical lines with Cartesian equations $u=\sqrt 2$ and $u=3,$ and

- two horizontal lines with Cartesian equations $v=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ and $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$

as shown in the diagram below.

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 3.$ 

Substituting $v=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$ 

Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. It lies between the first and second quadrants between the polar rays $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$

- Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=3$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$ 

Substituting $u=3$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(3\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. It lies between the first and second quadrants between the polar rays $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$

Therefore, the image $D$ of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=3,$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},$

"![](images/1f/1f899ac64f4d16cc14255603642e9038ec0b76f6b3ec27da53d3692b25431444.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

Find the image of $Δ$ under the action of $T.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we transform each side of $Δ$ separately:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $1\le u\le \sqrt{2}.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{\pi }{5}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{5})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{\pi }{5}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $\sqrt{2}$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the top side, where we have $v=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $1\le u\le \sqrt{2}.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{\pi }{3}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})).\end{aligned}
$$

This line segment makes an angle of $\frac{\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. Moreover, this segment lies on a line that passes through the origin, and its endpoints lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $\sqrt{2}$ centered at $O.$

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\frac{\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$

- Consider the image of the right side, where we have $u=\sqrt{2}$ and $\frac{\pi }{5}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Substituting $u=\sqrt{2}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$

Therefore, the image $D$ of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is the region that is enclosed between 

- two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=\sqrt{2},$ and

- two rays with polar equations $\theta =\frac{\pi }{5}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3},$

as shown in the diagram below.

Consider the rectangular region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  1 \le u \le 3, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq v \leq \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \right\},
$$

and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Determine the image of the top side of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $\Delta$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the top side.

For the top side, we have $v = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 3.$ 

Substituting $v = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})),\,1\le u\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the bottom side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

- The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis.
- The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis.
- The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O.$" :question/worked-solution "To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the bottom side.

For the bottom side, we have $v=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $1\le u\le \sqrt{2}.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})),\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/fc/fcfc165548d8174ec0468dce53317fd0c8daa14565852c5e44d6764161723bed.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement III is false.

- When $u=1,$ we obtain the point 
$(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})),$
whose distance to the origin is $1.$

- When $u=\sqrt{2},$ we obtain the point 
$(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})),$
whose distance to the origin is $\sqrt{2}.$

So, the endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186198595 :question/id #uuid "1d4e8a0e-128a-5dff-8f04-d70430a5470c" :question/math-academy-id "q-160890"} {:db/id 17592186278351 :question/id :step/math-academy-id 44184} {:db/id 17592186199277 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199463 :tutorial/content "Consider the rectangular region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
\Delta = \bigg\{ (u,v) \: :  \:  1 \le u \le 2, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5} \bigg\}
$$

and the transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

A sketch of $\Delta$ is shown below.

![](images/06/06abbcf6887f4b36ad85e4623a5c439f3613fdf7c2f3b342df2ff54fecbc86f6.png)

To find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ onto the $xy$-plane, we need to transform each side (bottom, top, left, and right) of $\Delta$ separately: 

![](images/06/062a3d1f13e8566770118650c92231ebe17f5eba2b4ae8d8b41722e33a72baff.png)

It can be shown that $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$ So, let's proceed to find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ by mapping these four sides." :tutorial/id #uuid "89fbd7db-7e0a-5047-9be9-1a886c8970f3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7615 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2e182722-189e-524f-a581-82e71805ddc4" :step/math-academy-id 44217 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199308}} {:db/id 17592186199278 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198377 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198019 :question/id #uuid "4eaf3262-b6e3-57bc-9662-42ab52626ee9" :question/math-academy-id "e-12340"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4068f861-26ff-582b-93c5-15f2fd44565d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198577} {:db/id 17592186198597} {:db/id 17592186278343} {:db/id 17592186278344} {:db/id 17592186278345} {:db/id 17592186389077} {:db/id 17592186389084} {:db/id 17592186389091}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Image of a Rectangle Under a Polar Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "c6da0258-e96c-5bbb-91d8-5c5aab571523" :step/math-academy-id 44222 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199279}} {:db/id 17592186199279 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199464 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following transformation:

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v), \qquad u > 0, \quad 0\leq v < 2\pi .
$$

If we substitute $u = r$ and $v = \theta,$ we get 

$$
\mathbf{T}:(r,\theta) \to (r \cos \theta, \, r \sin \theta), \qquad r > 0, \quad 0\leq\theta < 2\pi ,
$$

which we can write as

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad

Our goal is to find the image of the region $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).
$$

Let's first find the images of the horizontal sides:

- Consider the image of the bottom side, where we have $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$ Substituting $v=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(u\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,u\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})).\end{aligned}
$$

This represents a line segment that lies on a line passing through the origin. The slope of this line must be

$$
k = \dfrac{\sin \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)}{\cos \bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg)} = \tan\bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\bigg),
$$

meaning that the line makes an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis in the $xy$-plane. 
The endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/ca/ca644fa90870697e9cea1740c6432d43f682c650521217f19ea6f87c09cba0fd.png)

- Similarly, we can find the image of the top side, where $v=\dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ and $1 \leq u \leq 2.$

Our transformation $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\mathbf{T}:(u,v) \to (u \cos v, \, u \sin v).

- Consider the image of the left side, where we have $u=1$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq v \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{5}.$ Substituting $u=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y)=(\operatorname{cos}v,\,\operatorname{sin}v).\end{aligned}
$$

This is an arc of the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. The arc lies in the first quadrant between the polar rays $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{5},$ as shown below.

![](images/2e/2e0e5a723b7a9fdc860bcf3f619b6db4bdbec24c06bc22f3121a620080969b6c.png)

- two circles with polar equations $r=1$ and $r=2,$ and

as shown in the diagram below.

"Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
